newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks bob lower amid gloom on economy.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks bob lower amid gloom on economy.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key index bobbed wildly as it spent the day under water on Thursday, plunging 3.6 percent at one point before clawing back up in late trade to end just 1.32 percent down.

Brokers said a lack of confidence in Japan's economy and growing concerns that the government's tightening of fiscal policy will hinder economic growth sent the Tokyo Nikkei average of 225 leading shares into a free-fall, plummetting more than 700 points at one stage before rebounding to end 257.83 points lower at 19,291.58.
It dipped to 18,819.92 in the afternoon, its first time below the key 19,000 threshold since December 6, 1995.
"The fall today was a show of disapproval for Japan's budget (draft) for fiscal 1997," said Keiji Arai, a strategist at Sanyo Securities.
"The market thinks the future of the economy is going to be bleak and investors ceased buying, opting for the sidelines for most of the day," he said.

Late on Wednesday, Japan's cabinet approved a draft budget for fiscal 1997 with a tax rise of nearly seven trillion yen ($61.4 billion) and a delay in a corporate tax cut, sparking fears that a fledgling recovery in the economy may be damaged.
Already-fragile stocks were also dealt a blow on Thursday morning when the yen fell to a 44-month low against the dollar, fuelling fears of selling of stocks by foreign investors.
The negative sentiment also hit bonds, resulting in a triple-whammy for the Japanese markets, with losses in stocks, the yen and Japanese government bonds.
"A triple-loss means that there is little to look forward to in Japan's financial markets," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, general manager at Yamaichi Securities.
"The stock market was starting to digest the negative effects of the fiscal tightening when the yen suddenly fell, which sent the indices spiralling alarmingly lower," he added.
Brokers said a glut of technical factors, such as arbitrage-linked selling, were also a burden for the market.
Arbitrageurs simultaneously trade stocks and their underlying futures, and profit from momentary discrepancies between the prices of the two instruments.
Tokyo stocks had been fairly subdued for most of the year, but sentiment turned especially sour in early December.

On December 6, after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned of "irrational exuberance" in U.S. financial markets, the Nikkei posted its steepest single-day plunge of the year, by 667.20 points.
Greenspan's remarks were seen as a signal that the United States might raise interest rates to curb the markets' zeal, which could have a knock-on effect on Japanese markets.

Relatively upbeat comments on the domestic economy by government officials followed, but the stock market paid no heed, crashing through support levels and posting losses of nearly five percent in the course of three weeks.
Market participants have been waiting to see when the Nikkei average will stop falling.
Technical indicators have set off alarm bells that the market was being oversold, but brokers said investors seemed to think the market should fall as far as it wants.
If the weakness persists, the government could take measures to rescue the market, some said.
"It is too early to say but if the free-fall continues, something will need to be done," one strategist said.
A Finance Ministry official shrugged off the heavy losses.
"We are aware that stocks are falling, but the market level is something the market decides," he said.
